rationale: The book's central identification — lamp oil as stored, proven obedience rather than the Holy Spirit — is carried by the texts it cites and directly answers the strongest counter-reading. Its decisive move is exegetical, not rhetorical: in Matthew 25:9 the wise command the foolish to BUY oil, and the refusal to share is the pivot of the plot; Acts 8:20 establishes that the Spirit (the gift of God) cannot be purchased, and the same objection dispatches the grace and faith readings, since freely given gifts cannot be stored beforehand, kept in one's own vessel, or be un-lendable. The Spirit interpretation must treat the parable's hinge detail as disposable furniture; the book's reading makes it load-bearing and finds the exact command in Scripture ('Buy the truth,' Prov 23:23) with the price defined in Isaiah 55:1-3 as hearing and obeying, not money. The positive identification is likewise carried by the cited texts: Matthew 5:16, within the same gospel, explicitly defines the shining light as 'good works' seen by men, so what fuels the light is works; Proverbs 6:23 fixes lamp = commandment and light = law, leaving oil as the doing that turns the one into the other; Proverbs 21:20 places oil in the dwelling of the wise while the fool 'spendeth it up,' the very wise/fool + oil pairing of the parable; and Proverbs 13:9/24:20 ('the lamp of the wicked shall be put out') parallels the foolish virgins' own confession. The frame is secured by Matthew 7:24-27, in the same discourse tradition, where wise vs. foolish is defined precisely as doing vs. merely hearing — matching the book's claim that the foolish lack accumulated obedience, not the Spirit's presence. Exodus 27:20 (beaten olive oil for continual light) grounds the 'pressed, tested fruit' image, and Jeremiah 11:16 (Israel as olive tree) coheres with it. The common interpretation's strongest texts (1 Sam 16:13, Zech 4, Acts 10:38) concern anointing oil, not lamp oil, and the Spirit reading of Matthew 25 has always been an extension by convention that leaves the 'buy' and 'no lending' details unexplained. The book's speculative elements (Shem Tov Hebrew Matthew, the Gethsemane etymology) are supplementary color, not load-bearing for the oil identification.
decisive_sources: Matthew 25:9 with Acts 8:20 (oil must be bought; the Spirit cannot be)
Matthew 5:16 (the shining light is explicitly 'good works')
Proverbs 6:23 (lamp = commandment, law = light; oil is what makes the held commandment shine)
Proverbs 21:20 (oil in the dwelling of the wise; the fool spends it up)
Proverbs 23:23 with Isaiah 55:1-3 (buying truth/wisdom at the price of hearing and doing)
Proverbs 13:9 / 24:20 (the lamp of the wicked put out, matching the foolish virgins' confession)
Matthew 7:24-27 (wise vs. foolish defined as doing vs. hearing only, in the same discourse)
Exodus 27:20 (beaten olive oil for the light — pressed, proven produce stored for burning)
unresolved_objections: The entry's blanket claim 'not the Spirit' does not engage the anointing-oil texts (1 Samuel 16:13, Acts 10:38, Zechariah 4:6) where the oil–Spirit association is strongest; the book refutes the Spirit reading only in the lamp-oil context it treats
Reliance on Shem Tov's Hebrew Matthew ('bridegroom and bride,' 'lazy fools,' nid'akhu) rests on a late and disputed textual witness, though these details are not load-bearing

A defender of the Spirit reading could still argue that parable details like 'buy' should not be pressed allegorically, though the book's counter that the refusal and purchase are the plot's hinge is reasonable
